title: Real-time translation for remote teams: a practical guide
excerpt: Real-time translation for remote teams removes the language barrier from daily calls. Here is how it works and how to roll it out.
author: VoxTranslate Team
content:
Distributed teams are global by default, but most video tools still assume everyone shares one language. Real-time translation for remote teams closes that gap: each person speaks their own language and everyone else reads — and hears — the conversation in theirs, live. This guide explains how it works and how to introduce it without disrupting your workflow.

Why language is the hidden tax on remote work

When part of a team works in a second language, meetings slow down, quieter voices stay quiet, and nuance gets lost. The cost is rarely measured, but it shows up as repeated questions, longer threads, and decisions that have to be revisited. Removing that friction is one of the highest-leverage changes a global team can make.

How real-time translation works on a call

VoxTranslate runs a continuous loop for every speaker: it captures the audio in the browser, transcribes it as you talk, translates it into every language present in the room, and delivers the result as live subtitles — plus a natural spoken translation on higher tiers.

  • Speak naturally: no need to slow down or simplify your sentences.
  • Read along: live subtitles appear in each listener's own language.
  • Hear it too: Premium speaks a natural AI translation.

Choosing the right setup for your team

VoxTranslate lets you pick an engine per call, so you can match speed and quality to the moment:

  • Standard — fast and economical for daily stand-ups and casual syncs.
  • Enhanced — client-direct streaming with roughly sub-250ms latency for fast back-and-forth.
  • Premium — the highest-fidelity option with full 84-language coverage for high-stakes conversations.

Rolling it out without friction

Because VoxTranslate is browser-native, there is nothing to install — share a room link, allow the microphone and camera, and you are in. A few tips for adoption:

  1. Start with one recurring meeting where language is a known pain point.
  2. Let people set their own language; the source is auto-detected anyway.
  3. Use the auto-translated text chat for links and follow-ups during the call.
  4. Download the session transcript afterwards so non-native speakers can review at their own pace.

Privacy and cost considerations

Video and audio flow peer-to-peer over WebRTC and are not recorded or routed through servers. Billing is credit-based: you start with free credits and pay per minute of speech, with no subscription, so a small team can trial it on real meetings before committing.

Frequently asked questions

Does real-time translation slow down meetings?

No. Subtitles appear as you speak, and the Enhanced tier targets roughly sub-250ms latency, so conversations keep their natural rhythm instead of stalling for interpretation.

How many people can join a translated call?

VoxTranslate uses a peer-to-peer mesh with up to four participants per call, with every language in the room translated in parallel.

Is the translation accurate enough for work?

It is built for everyday communication and works well for most conversations, but AI translation can contain errors and the spoken output is computer-generated, so it should not be relied on for critical legal, medical, or safety decisions.

title: How to host a multilingual video meeting (step by step)
excerpt: Hosting a multilingual video meeting is simple with live translation. Follow these steps to run a call where everyone understands each other.
author: VoxTranslate Team
content:
Running a multilingual video meeting used to mean booking an interpreter or hoping everyone could cope in a shared second language. With live translation built into the call, you can host one in minutes. Here is a step-by-step guide to a meeting where every participant speaks and listens in their own language.

Before the meeting

Preparation is light, but a couple of choices up front make the call smoother:

  • Pick your engine: Standard for casual syncs, Premium when you want a natural spoken translation for clients.
  • Share the room link in the invite so people can join straight from the browser — no install required.
  • Remind guests to allow microphone and camera access when they join.

Step 1: Create or open the room

Open VoxTranslate in the browser and start a room. You can keep it private and share the code, or use a public room. Signing in unlocks billing and saved preferences; guests can join too, depending on the room.

Step 2: Set each person's language

Everyone chooses the language they want to speak and hear. The source language is auto-detected, so people can simply start talking, but it can also be set manually if you prefer certainty.

Step 3: Speak naturally and watch the subtitles

As each person talks, their words are transcribed and translated live into every language in the room. Listeners see subtitles in their own language, and on Premium they also hear a natural AI voice translation.

Step 4: Use the in-call tools

A multilingual meeting is more than audio. During the call you can:

  • Send messages in the auto-translated text chat.
  • Share your screen or sketch on the collaborative whiteboard.
  • Use emoji reactions and hand-raise to keep large calls orderly.

Step 5: Follow up afterwards

When the call ends, download the session transcript in the language you want, generate an AI report, and email a recap to participants so nothing gets lost in translation after the fact.

Frequently asked questions

Do participants need to install anything?

No. VoxTranslate is browser-native — guests open the room link, allow mic and camera, and they are in.

How many languages can one meeting handle?

Every language present in the room is translated in parallel, so a four-person call can run in four different languages at once.

Can I get a record of what was said?

Yes. You can download the transcript (in your chosen language) and downloadable session reports in formats like PDF, JSON, SRT, and VTT.

title: AI voice translation vs. Google Translate: which to use
excerpt: AI voice translation vs Google Translate: one is built for live spoken conversations, the other for text. Here is how to choose.
author: VoxTranslate Team
content:
If you have ever pasted a sentence into Google Translate during a call, you already know the workaround is clumsy. The real question in the AI voice translation vs Google Translate debate is not which is better overall — it is which tool fits the job. They are built for different things.

What Google Translate is great at

Google Translate is excellent for text. It shines when you need to:

  • Translate a typed message, document, or web page.
  • Look up a single word or phrase quickly.
  • Handle asynchronous, one-off translation where timing does not matter.

It is free, fast, and ubiquitous — a brilliant utility for written, on-demand translation.

What live AI voice translation is built for

A live conversation is a different problem. AI voice translation is purpose-built for multi-person spoken calls: it transcribes each speaker in real time, translates into every language in the room at once, and delivers subtitles plus a natural spoken translation — without anyone copying and pasting.

  • Real-time: subtitles appear as you speak.
  • Multi-party: several languages in one room, translated in parallel.
  • Spoken output: higher tiers voice the translation so you can listen, not just read.

Side by side

Think of it as text-first vs conversation-first:

  1. Input: Google Translate expects typed text; VoxTranslate listens to live speech.
  2. Timing: one is asynchronous; the other is real-time during a call.
  3. People: one translates for you; the other translates a whole multilingual room.
  4. Output: text on a screen vs subtitles plus a spoken voice in the call.

Which should you choose?

Use Google Translate for written, one-off translation and quick lookups. Use a dedicated live tool like VoxTranslate when people need to actually talk to each other across languages — meetings, interviews, support, and social calls. Many people use both: Translate for the email, VoxTranslate for the conversation.

A note on accuracy

Both rely on AI, and AI translation can contain errors. VoxTranslate's spoken translation is computer-generated, not a recording of the speaker, and neither tool should be relied on for critical legal, medical, or safety decisions.

Frequently asked questions

Can Google Translate handle a live video call?

Not natively as a multi-person call experience. It is designed for text and quick spoken phrases, whereas VoxTranslate is built to translate an entire live conversation with subtitles and spoken output.

Is AI voice translation free?

VoxTranslate is credit-based with free starter credits and pay-per-minute usage, while Google Translate is free for text. The right choice depends on whether you need live conversation or one-off text.

How many languages do they support?

VoxTranslate supports 84 languages, with its Premium tier powered by Google Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, which covers 70+ languages and 2,000+ language combinations.

title: Live subtitles explained: real-time captions on calls
excerpt: Live subtitles turn speech into on-screen captions in real time. Here is how they work and why they make video calls clearer.
author: VoxTranslate Team
content:
Live subtitles have quietly become one of the most useful features on a video call. They turn spoken words into on-screen text the instant they are said — and when paired with translation, they let people follow a conversation in a language they do not speak. This article explains how live subtitles work and why they matter.

What live subtitles actually are

Live subtitles are real-time captions generated from speech as it happens, rather than added afterwards. On a translated call they go one step further: the caption appears in each listener's own language, not just the speaker's.

How real-time captioning works

The pipeline behind live subtitles runs continuously while you talk:

  1. Capture: your browser streams short, low-latency chunks of audio.
  2. Transcribe: streaming speech recognition converts audio to text as you speak.
  3. Translate: the text is translated into every language in the room.
  4. Display: each participant sees captions in the language they chose.

Why live subtitles improve every call

Captions are not only for translation. They make calls clearer and more inclusive for everyone:

  • Accessibility for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.
  • Clarity in noisy environments or with imperfect audio.
  • Comprehension for non-native speakers who read faster than they listen.
  • A written record you can export as a transcript afterwards.

Subtitles plus spoken translation

Reading is great, but sometimes you want to listen. On VoxTranslate's Premium tier, the same translated text is also spoken aloud in a natural AI voice, so participants can choose to read the subtitles, hear the translation, or both.

From live captions to a transcript

Because the captions are generated as structured text, the whole conversation can be downloaded afterwards. You can export the transcript in the language you want, and add optional AI autocorrection for an even cleaner result.

Frequently asked questions

Are live subtitles the same as translated subtitles?

Not quite. Live subtitles caption what is said in real time; translated subtitles show those captions in another language. VoxTranslate does both at once.

How accurate are real-time captions?

They are good enough for everyday conversation, but because they are AI-generated they can contain errors, so they should not be relied on for critical decisions.

Can I save the subtitles after the call?

Yes. You can download the transcript in your chosen language, with optional AI autocorrection for a polished version.

title: How to host a multilingual webinar with live translation
excerpt: Broadcast to an international audience without booking interpreters: what a live-translated webinar is, how to set one up, and exactly what your attendees see and hear in their own language.
author: VoxTranslate Team
content:
A webinar reaches people who do not share your language. Usually that means one of three compromises: run the session in English and lose the room, repeat it once per region, or hire simultaneous interpreters. A live-translated webinar removes the choice — you present once, in your own language, and every attendee follows along in theirs.

A webinar is not a meeting

The distinction matters, because the two work differently. A VoxTranslate meeting is a small peer-to-peer call: everyone speaks, everyone is translated, up to four people. A webinar is a broadcast: one host presents to an audience of any size, and the audience watches rather than talks. Because it is one-to-many, the audience needs no camera, no microphone, and no account — just a link.

Before you go live

Pick the source language, not the audience's

You set the language you will speak. Translation flows outward from there, so present in the language you are most fluent and most persuasive in. Your accent, your idioms and your pace are all easier to work with when you are not translating in your head.

Decide who can join

Every webinar gets a short join link and a QR code. A private webinar is reachable only by that link — good for customer training or an internal all-hands. A public one is also listed in the app, which is what you want for open sessions you are actively promoting. If the session should be restricted to signed-in members, that too is a switch, not a workaround.

Schedule it, or start now

You can open a webinar immediately or schedule it, which gives you a calendar entry to share and reminders for attendees. For anything you are promoting in advance, schedule it: the link stays stable, so it can go into the invite, the newsletter and the landing page long before you go live.

Going live

As host you publish your microphone, and optionally your camera. That is the whole setup — there is no software to install for you or for your audience, because the broadcast runs in the browser. Speech recognition transcribes you as you talk, and the transcript is translated in parallel into every language present in the room, so a session with attendees across five languages is handled at once rather than five times.

What your audience actually gets

  • Live subtitles in their own language, chosen per person — nobody has to settle for a shared second language.
  • Spoken translation, so attendees can listen instead of reading a transcript while also watching your slides.
  • Translated chat. A question typed in Portuguese reaches you in your language, and your answer reaches the room in theirs. This is where multilingual webinars usually break down, and it is the part most worth having.
  • No account, no download. Attendees open the link, pick a display name, and they are in. Every extra step between an invite and a live face costs you attendance.

Five things worth doing

  1. Speak in complete sentences. Recognition and translation both work on clause boundaries; trailing off mid-thought is the main cause of an awkward subtitle.
  2. Say product names deliberately. Proper nouns are the hardest thing for any transcription system. Slow down half a beat on yours.
  3. Pause after questions. Translation and speech take a moment to arrive. A two-second pause is the difference between a conversation and people talking over the translation.
  4. Put the link and QR code on your last slide. Attendees who arrive late or want to share it with a colleague will look for it there.
  5. Enable the transcript if you plan a recap. A multilingual transcript is a follow-up email, a blog post and a searchable record for the people who could not attend.

Where this pays off

The pattern is the same for a product launch, a partner briefing, a customer training session or a company all-hands: an audience that spans languages, a message you only want to deliver once, and questions you actually want to receive — including from the people whose English would have kept them silent.

A note on AI output

Transcription and translation are produced by AI systems and can contain mistakes, and the spoken translation attendees hear is computer-generated rather than a recording of your voice. For everyday business communication that trade-off is easily worth it; for legally binding or safety-critical proceedings, a human interpreter is still the right call.

title: Choosing a multilingual webinar platform: a buyer’s checklist
excerpt: Nine questions that separate a platform that genuinely works across languages from one that only advertises it: latency, attendee friction, translated chat, transcripts, pricing.
author: VoxTranslate Team
content:
Every platform in this category says it supports live translation. The differences only show up on the day you run a real session for a real audience — which is a bad time to find them. These are the questions that decide whether a multilingual webinar works, in the order they tend to hurt.

1. How much delay is there between you speaking and the audience understanding?

This is the number that determines whether questions and answers feel like a conversation. Latency of a second or two is workable. Six or seven seconds is not: the audience stops asking anything, because by the time an answer arrives the moment has passed. Ask for the end-to-end figure — speech to translated output — not the transcription latency alone.

2. What does an attendee have to install or sign up for?

Every step between your invite and a live attendee costs you people, and the cost is highest on mobile. A link that opens in the browser is the benchmark. A required download, a required account, or a required plugin all quietly reduce your audience — and the reduction is invisible, so it never gets attributed to the tool.

3. Does each attendee choose their own language?

There is a real difference between "the webinar is translated into Spanish" and "each attendee picks the language they want". The first forces you to know your audience's languages in advance and run separate sessions when you are wrong. The second scales to whoever shows up.

4. Is there spoken translation, or only subtitles?

Subtitles compete with your slides for the same pair of eyes. For a demo or a technical walkthrough, that is a real problem: attendees can read you or watch you, not both. Translated audio lets them listen to you and look at what you are showing.

5. Is the chat translated?

This is the question most buyers forget, and the one that decides whether your webinar is a broadcast or a conversation. If chat is untranslated, questions arrive in languages you cannot answer and the quieter half of your audience stays quiet. Check that questions reach you in your language and that your answers reach each person in theirs.

6. What happens to the recording and the transcript?

Most of the value of a webinar arrives after it ends: the follow-up, the internal recap, the clip for people in the wrong time zone. Ask whether a transcript is produced, whether it is available in more than the source language, and whether you can export it. A recording nobody can search is an archive, not an asset.

7. How does it handle your vocabulary?

Product names, feature names and industry jargon are where translation quality visibly fails, and they are exactly the words your webinar is about. Ask what control you have — a glossary, a terminology list, anything — and test with your own product names rather than a generic script.

8. How does the price scale?

Three models are common, and they behave very differently as you grow: per interpreter and hour (predictable, expensive, needs booking), per seat (cheap until your audience grows), and per minute of use (scales with actual usage). Model your real calendar — a monthly all-hands plus ad-hoc customer sessions — rather than comparing headline prices.

9. Where does your audio go?

A webinar can carry unreleased roadmap, customer names or financials. Ask what is retained, for how long, who can access it, and whether recording and transcription are opt-in per session. "It's encrypted" answers a different question than the one you asked.

How VoxTranslate answers these

Attendees join a link in the browser with no account and no download, and each one picks their own language for subtitles and spoken translation. Chat is translated both ways, so questions arrive in your language and your answers land in theirs. Sessions can be private or public, scheduled with reminders, and restricted to signed-in members when the content calls for it. Transcription is opt-in per webinar rather than on by default.

Transcription and translation are AI-generated and can contain mistakes — worth knowing before you use any tool in this category for legally binding or safety-critical proceedings.

title: Global product launches and all-hands: one webinar, every language
excerpt: Regional repeat sessions and interpreter booths are how multilingual launches have always been run. Live-translated webinars replace both — here is what actually changes.
author: VoxTranslate Team
content:
There are two traditional ways to present to an audience that does not share your language, and both are expensive. You can repeat the session per region — three time zones, three rehearsals, three slightly different messages — or you can hire simultaneous interpreters, which works well and costs enough that it is reserved for the biggest moments. Most companies quietly choose a third option: run it in English and accept that part of the audience disengages.

What changes with a single broadcast

A live-translated webinar collapses those repeats into one session. You present once. Each attendee reads subtitles and hears speech in their own language, and asks questions in it too. Three consequences follow, and they are worth stating plainly:

  • One message, not three. Repeat sessions drift. The third run is never the first run, and the version each region heard is the version they will quote back to you.
  • Questions from people who would not have asked. Attendees will ask in writing in their own language what they would never have asked out loud in a second one.
  • Attendance from people who would not have come. A session advertised as "with live translation into your language" converts differently from one advertised in English.

Product launches

A launch has a date, and the date is the same everywhere. Announcing simultaneously to every market — instead of staggering by region while the news leaks — keeps the story intact. Practical notes: put your product names on a slide as well as saying them, since proper nouns are where any translation system struggles; and keep the demo slower than usual, because attendees are splitting attention between your screen and their subtitles.

Company all-hands

Internal communication is where the language barrier costs the most and is measured the least. When the quarterly all-hands is in a language half the company reads at a professional but not comfortable level, the result is not confusion — it is silence: no questions, no pushback, no signal. Live translation changes who speaks up. Make the Q&A chat explicitly multilingual by answering the first question in the language it was asked in; that single move gives everyone else permission.

Customer training and onboarding

Training is the clearest financial case, because it repeats. A weekly onboarding session that previously ran per language now runs once. Enable the transcript: a multilingual transcript becomes your follow-up email, your help-centre article and the asset for customers who could not attend live — which is most of them.

Partner and reseller briefings

Partner networks are international by definition, and partners are the people you least want operating on a stale or half-understood version of your roadmap. A single briefing everyone can follow in their own language beats a deck emailed with "let me know if you have questions", which is how briefings quietly fail.

Running the session well

  1. Rehearse with translation on. Presenting with live subtitles running is a slightly different skill: shorter sentences, cleaner clause endings, fewer trailing thoughts.
  2. Announce the languages in the invite. Attendees do not assume a webinar will be understandable in their language — tell them, and watch registrations from non-English-speaking markets move.
  3. Share the link and QR code early. A stable join link can sit in the invite, the newsletter and the reminder without changing.
  4. Pause after every question. Speech and translation need a beat to land. The pause that feels awkward to you is what makes the session work for everyone else.
  5. Plan the follow-up before you go live. Decide what the recap is — transcript, clip, summary — while you can still set the recording options.

Measuring it

The signals worth watching are which languages your attendees actually chose, how many questions arrived in something other than your source language, and attendance from markets you previously reached with an English-only session. The first two tell you where your audience really is; the third tells you what the language barrier was costing you.

A note on AI output

Transcription and translation are AI-generated and can contain mistakes, and the spoken translation is synthesized rather than a recording of the speaker. For launches, all-hands and training that trade-off is straightforward. For legally binding or safety-critical proceedings, use a human interpreter.

title: Real-time translation in Zoom, Teams and Meet: the options and their limits
excerpt: Your company standardised on Zoom, Teams or Meet — and now you need a meeting nobody has to hold in a second language. Here are the three honest options, what each one costs you, and how to choose.
author: VoxTranslate Team
content:
Your company already has a video platform. Then a customer, a partner or half a new team turns out not to share your language, and the question arrives: can we just translate the meeting we already run? The honest answer is that you have three options, they are genuinely different, and the right one depends on the meeting rather than the platform.

Option 1: built-in translated captions

Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet all offer some form of translated captions. It is the path of least resistance — same tool, same invite, no new vendor — and for a session where the audience mostly needs the gist, it is often enough.

What to check before you rely on it, because all three differ and change over time:

  • Is it on your plan? Translated captions are typically a higher-tier or add-on feature rather than part of the base licence.
  • Which language pairs? Coverage is usually narrower than the marketing suggests, and the pair you need may not be there.
  • Text only? Built-in captions give you subtitles. Nobody in the meeting hears a translation, which matters more than it sounds — see below.
  • Does it work in the browser? External guests without the desktop app sometimes lose the feature entirely.

Option 2: interpreters, in the platform or in a booth

All three platforms support interpretation channels: you bring human interpreters, they get their own audio channel, attendees pick a language. Quality is the highest available — a good interpreter conveys tone, hesitation and intent, not just words — and for a shareholder meeting, a regulated proceeding or a negotiation where a nuance is worth money, it remains the right choice.

The cost is booking. Interpreters are scheduled in advance, priced per hour and per language pair, and do not scale to a Tuesday stand-up or a support call that just happened to arrive in Portuguese. Most companies end up reserving interpretation for a handful of events a year and quietly doing nothing for everything else.

Option 3: hold the meeting in a tool built for it

The third option is to run the specific meeting somewhere designed around translation instead of adding translation to a tool designed around one shared language. Being direct about what that means: VoxTranslate is not a plugin for Zoom, Teams or Meet. It is its own room — you send a link and people join in the browser. If your requirement is "inside our existing platform, no exceptions", options 1 and 2 are your shortlist and you can stop here.

What you get for using a separate room:

  • Everyone speaks their own language, not just one presenter being translated for the others.
  • Spoken translation, not only subtitles. Subtitles and a shared screen compete for the same pair of eyes; during a demo, attendees can read you or watch you, not both.
  • Translated chat, so a question typed in one language arrives in yours and your answer lands in theirs.
  • A glossary. Product names and jargon are where translation quality visibly breaks; a term list is injected as mandatory terminology so your vocabulary survives.
  • Nothing to install for external guests, and no account for webinar attendees.

Choosing, in practice

  1. Internal meeting, everyone on your platform, gist is enough? Built-in captions. Don't add a vendor for this.
  2. High-stakes, legally consequential or press-facing? Human interpreters. AI output can contain mistakes, and here that matters.
  3. Recurring, multi-language, and you need people to actually talk? A dedicated translated room. Sales calls, support, onboarding, partner briefings and all-hands are where the difference shows up — precisely the sessions that repeat, where booking interpreters never happens.

A hybrid that works

Most teams land somewhere in the middle, and that is fine: keep your platform for the default calendar, and use a translated room for the meetings where language is the actual constraint. The invite is a link, so switching for one meeting costs nothing and commits you to nothing.

A note on AI output

Transcription and translation — in any tool in this category, built-in captions included — are produced by AI and can contain mistakes, and synthesized speech is not a recording of the speaker's voice. For everyday business communication that is a reasonable trade. For legally binding or safety-critical proceedings, use a human interpreter.

title: Where does your meeting audio go? A privacy checklist for AI translation
excerpt: Live translation means your meeting audio leaves the room. Seven questions to ask any vendor about retention, sub-processors and recordings — and VoxTranslate’s answers to each.
author: VoxTranslate Team
content:
Live translation only works if something processes your speech, which means your meeting audio leaves the room. That is not a scandal — it is how the technology works — but it does mean the questions below belong in your evaluation, not in a security review six months after rollout. Your meetings carry unreleased roadmap, customer names, salary discussions and pricing. Ask.

1. Is raw audio stored, or only processed?

There is a large difference between "we process your audio" and "we keep your audio". Ask specifically whether the raw stream is retained anywhere after the sentence is transcribed, and for how long.

VoxTranslate: speech is streamed for transcription and translation while you talk and is not stored. What can persist is text, not audio.

2. Who else is in the chain?

Nobody in this category runs the entire stack alone: speech recognition, translation and speech synthesis are usually separate providers. Ask for the named sub-processor list — not the phrase "trusted partners" — and check it against your own DPA obligations.

VoxTranslate: which provider is involved depends on the engine tier chosen for the session — speech recognition, translation and speech synthesis are separate services, and on one tier the browser streams audio directly to the provider without passing through our server at all. The providers, and what each one receives, are published in the privacy policy.

3. What happens to transcripts?

Transcripts are the part that actually accumulates, and they are a written record of everything said. Ask whether they are stored by default, who can read them, whether they can be exported, and whether they are deleted with the account.

VoxTranslate: transcripts are stored for calls in which a signed-in user took part, so participants can review, export (PDF/JSON) and correct them afterwards. Calls with only guests are not stored. Stored transcripts are deleted when you delete your account.

4. Does the video pass through their servers?

This one is easy to skip and worth asking, because architecture beats policy: media that never reaches a server cannot be retained by one.

VoxTranslate: in meetings, video and audio travel peer-to-peer between browsers over WebRTC and are not routed through or recorded by the server. When a direct connection is impossible, media is relayed encrypted in a form the relay cannot read. The server handles sign-in, signaling, the speech-to-text stream, translation and chat relay.

5. Is recording opt-in — and can participants tell?

Ask whether recording and transcript retention are per-session switches or account-wide defaults, and what participants see when either is on. In several jurisdictions notice is not a courtesy, it is the law.

VoxTranslate: for webinars, video recording and transcript capture are per-session options rather than always-on defaults.

6. Can you actually get data deleted?

"You can request deletion" and "here is the button" are different products. Ask what a deletion covers — account, transcripts, past sessions — and how long it takes.

VoxTranslate: deleting your account deletes your stored transcripts and your utterances along with it.

7. What is the legal basis, and where?

For EU deployments, ask which legal basis is claimed for processing meeting audio, where processing happens, and how international transfers are handled. A vendor that cannot answer quickly has not thought about it.

VoxTranslate: processing audio for live captions and translation is covered by contract plus the consent given at sign-up; the details and the transfer position are in the privacy policy rather than paraphrased in marketing copy.

Two questions worth adding for your own side

  • Who in your company can read a transcript? The vendor's answer is only half of it. A stored transcript of a compensation discussion is a document your own access rules now have to cover.
  • What should not be translated live? Decide the exceptions in advance — legal proceedings, incident calls, anything under embargo — rather than during them.

A note on AI output

Transcription and translation are AI-generated and can contain mistakes, and spoken translation is synthesized rather than a recording of the speaker. That has a privacy implication people miss: an imperfect transcript is still a record, and it can misattribute or garble what someone said. Treat transcripts as useful, not as evidence.

title: Multilingual sales calls: selling across languages without an interpreter
excerpt: Your prospect is more precise and more candid in their own language. How to run discovery, demos and negotiation across languages — and where a human interpreter still wins.
author: VoxTranslate Team
content:
There is a version of every prospect that only exists in their own language: more precise about the problem, more candid about the budget, more willing to admit what they don't control. English-language discovery calls give you the polished version — the one that says "interesting" instead of "this will never get past our security team". If you sell internationally, that gap is costing you deals you never learn about.

Discovery is the stage that benefits most

Discovery is pure information gathering, which makes it the stage where a language barrier does the most damage and where live translation pays back fastest. Let the prospect speak their own language and you get the detail that qualification depends on: who else has to approve, what they tried before, what actually broke.

What changes in practice:

  • They stop simplifying. People compress when working in a second language — they give you the headline and drop the caveats. The caveats are your qualification criteria.
  • Objections arrive early. An objection someone cannot phrase comfortably becomes silence, and silence becomes a stalled deal three weeks later.
  • You hear who else matters. Buying committees get described in throwaway asides — exactly the part that gets cut in a second language.

Demos: slower, and with the vocabulary handled

A demo is the hardest call to translate well, for two reasons worth planning around.

First, attention splits. Your prospect is reading subtitles or listening to a translation while also watching your screen. So slow down, narrate what you are about to do before you do it, and pause on each screen a beat longer than feels natural.

Second, product vocabulary. Feature names, plan names and industry jargon are exactly where machine translation goes wrong — and exactly the words a demo is made of. Put your terminology into a glossary before the call: term pairs saved there are injected into the translation as mandatory terminology, so "Workspace" stays "Workspace" instead of becoming a literal translation nobody recognises.

Follow-up: the transcript is the deal note

A translated call produces something a normal call does not: a written record of what was said, available to both sides. Two uses:

  1. Your notes write themselves. Export the transcript and pull the exact phrasing your prospect used for their problem — then reuse their words in the proposal. Nothing lands like a buyer's own description of their pain.
  2. They can re-read it. Send the recap knowing your champion can forward something their colleagues can actually read in their language, which is how internal selling happens after you leave the call.

Which tier for which call

Match the engine to the stakes rather than defaulting to the cheapest or the best:

  • Standard — inbound qualification and quick check-ins where subtitles are enough.
  • Enhanced — fast back-and-forth discovery: the low-latency path, close to a natural conversational rhythm, and it can speak in a voice cloned per speaker.
  • Premium — the highest-fidelity option for the calls that decide the deal.

The stage where you still want a human

Contract negotiation. When the exact wording of a liability cap or an exclusivity clause is what is being discussed, use a human interpreter — and put the agreed text in writing, reviewed by both sides, in both languages. AI translation is built for conversation, and a conversation about legally binding wording is not the place to accept "close enough". Everything up to that point — discovery, demo, technical validation, security review, pricing — is exactly where it works.

Five habits that make translated sales calls work

  1. Open in their language. One sentence is enough: it signals the call is theirs to speak in, and it changes how the next thirty minutes go.
  2. One question at a time. Stacked questions ("what's your timeline, and who signs off, and what's the budget?") lose their middle in any translation.
  3. Confirm numbers out loud. Repeat prices, dates and seat counts and get explicit agreement. Numbers are where a misheard word costs real money.
  4. Use the chat for anything spelled. Domains, emails, SKUs and part numbers belong in the translated chat, not in speech.
  5. Ask "what did I miss?" at the end. In their language, in writing, with a pause. It is the single highest-yield question on a cross-language call.

A note on AI output

Transcription and translation are AI-generated and can contain mistakes, and the spoken translation is synthesized rather than a recording of the speaker. For commercial conversations that is a workable trade — but confirm anything that will end up in a contract in writing, in both languages.

title: How good is AI translation for business meetings — and where it fails
excerpt: An honest look at what live AI translation gets right, the five situations where it visibly breaks, and what you can actually do about each one before your next multilingual meeting.
author: VoxTranslate Team
content:
"Is it good enough?" is the right question to ask about live AI translation, and the honest answer has a shape: very good for ordinary business conversation, unreliable in five specific situations that are predictable enough to plan around. Anyone who tells you it is flawless is selling; anyone who tells you it is useless has not used a current system. Here is where the line actually falls.

What it does well

Ordinary spoken business language — status updates, discovery questions, technical explanation, support conversations, training — translates well enough that participants stop noticing the mechanism and get on with the meeting. That is the bar that matters, and it is routinely met. The pipeline is worth understanding, because each stage has its own failure mode: your speech is transcribed, the transcript is translated into every language present, and the result is delivered as subtitles and — depending on the tier — spoken aloud.

Failure 1: bad audio

Every downstream stage inherits the quality of the transcription, and transcription inherits the quality of your microphone. A laptop mic in a reverberant room with a fan running is the single most common cause of translation that "doesn't work" — and no model fixes it after the fact.

What to do: a headset, per person, in any meeting that matters. It outperforms every other quality intervention on this list, and it is the cheapest.

Failure 2: proper nouns and jargon

Product names, feature names, company names and industry terms are the words machine translation handles worst, and they are disproportionately the words your meeting is about. A feature called "Pulse" gets translated as a heartbeat, and the sentence stops making sense.

What to do: use a glossary. Term pairs saved for the room are injected into the translation as mandatory terminology, which keeps your vocabulary intact instead of hoping the model recognises it. Say proper nouns half a beat slower, and put them on screen too.

Failure 3: people talking over each other

Overlapping speech degrades transcription for everyone involved, and a translated call amplifies the cost: the crosstalk gets garbled, and because listeners are a moment behind, they cannot tell who was interrupted.

What to do: one speaker at a time, and a deliberate pause after questions. The pause that feels awkward to the speaker is what makes the meeting work for everyone reading a translation. On larger sessions, use hand-raise instead of "just jump in".

Failure 4: idioms, humour and code-switching

Idioms translate literally and land strangely. Sarcasm loses its marker and can invert your meaning. And code-switching — starting a sentence in one language and finishing it in another, or dropping in English technical terms mid-sentence — confuses the language detection that everything downstream depends on.

What to do: say what you mean rather than what is idiomatic ("we should decide this week" beats "let's get the ball rolling"). Keep sarcasm out of cross-language meetings; it costs more than it earns. If your team habitually mixes languages, agree on one language per speaker for the call.

Failure 5: anything where exact wording is the point

Contract language, regulatory statements, medical instructions, safety procedures. Here "approximately right" is not a partial success, it is a defect, and a fluent-sounding translation is more dangerous than an obviously broken one — nobody double-checks a sentence that reads well.

What to do: a human interpreter, plus the agreed text in writing in both languages. This is not a limitation to work around; it is the correct boundary of the tool.

Latency is part of quality

A perfect translation that arrives seven seconds late has already failed the conversation: people stop asking questions, because the moment has passed by the time the answer lands. Around a second or two keeps the rhythm of a real exchange. If you are evaluating tools, measure end-to-end delay — speech to translated output — on a real call, not the transcription latency quoted on the pricing page.

Choosing a tier is choosing a trade-off

VoxTranslate lets you pick per call, which is worth using deliberately: Standard for economical everyday sessions with subtitles, Enhanced for the lowest-latency back-and-forth (client-direct, and able to speak in a voice cloned per speaker), and Premium for the highest fidelity on the conversations that decide something. A daily stand-up and a board update do not need the same setting.

How to evaluate it for your own meetings

  1. Test with your own vocabulary. A generic demo script proves nothing — your product names are the hard part.
  2. Test with your actual accents. Recognition quality varies by speaker; use the people who will really be on the calls.
  3. Test the messy case. Two people interrupting each other on a bad connection is the real world, not a scripted monologue.
  4. Read a transcript afterwards. It shows you exactly what the system heard, which tells you more than any impression of the live call.
  5. Decide your exceptions. Write down which meetings will never be AI-translated, before someone has to decide mid-call.

A note on AI output

Transcription and translation are AI-generated and can contain mistakes, and spoken translation is synthesized rather than a recording of the speaker's voice. VoxTranslate is built for everyday communication — not for critical legal, medical or safety decisions.
